pages.title: Programming the sequencer
pages.caption: A producer does not replay the same drum pattern by hand every night. They program it into a sequencer once and let it run when needed. Start with a manual automation so you can test the prompt safely before giving it a schedule or trigger.

pages.title: The sequencer’s table
pages.caption: Programmed pattern: saved prompt. Hit play: manual trigger. Run on the clock: schedule. Chosen instruments: selected tools. Producer checks the mix: human reviews the result.

pages.title: A saved agent run
pages.caption: An automation has four beginner-friendly parts. Trigger: what starts it? Prompt: what should the agent do? Tools: what is the least access needed? Review path: where do I inspect the result?

pages.title: Start manual and local
pages.caption: A manual automation runs only when you start it. Keep it local while you test it. You can test the prompt, inspect output, adjust scope, avoid surprise runs, and confirm tools are minimal. Add a schedule, an event trigger, or cloud execution only after the manual prompt gives trustworthy results.

pages.title: A good starter automation
pages.caption: Pick work you already do more than once: "Which pull requests are blocked, and what do they need next?" Avoid first automations that write code, post comments, change labels, approve reviews, or merge pull requests. Automations are saved in the app, not committed with the repository. Keep secrets out of the prompt, and give the automation only the tools it needs.

pages.title: Confirm work items exist
pages.caption: Select **Pull requests** in the sidebar, then **Authored by me**, and add your fork’s `repo:` term to that tab’s query. You should see at least three open pull requests from the Chapter 00 setup script. The report shows whatever state your pull requests are in now. If the list is empty, run the script before continuing.

pages.title: A manual review readiness report
pages.caption: Open **Automations** and select **New automation**. Name it `PR review readiness report`. Change the **Trigger** from **Daily** to **Manual**, and make sure **Run in the cloud** is off. Paste the prompt, use **Select repository** to choose your fork, and select **Current checkout** in the **Workspace** picker. Select the arrow next to **Create**, then **Create and run**.

pages.title: The report’s prompt
pages.caption: For each open pull request in this repository, report: the PR number, title, and branch; the CI check status and the name of any failing check; whether there are unresolved review comments; whether the branch is up to date with the default branch; and the single next human action needed to move it toward merge. Present the results as a table. Do not edit files, add comments, change labels, approve reviews, or merge anything.

pages.title: Read the run
pages.caption: Wait for the run to complete. Open the run detail and confirm: the prompt matches what you pasted, no error text appears, and the result includes a table of open pull requests with CI status, comment status, and the next action for each. Your PR numbers, titles, and statuses may differ. Unlike the **Pull requests** view, this report explains why a PR is blocked, not only that it exists.

pages.title: Put it on the clock
pages.caption: Select the automation, then **Edit**. Change the **Trigger** from **Manual** to **Daily**. In **Hours**, select a time before your workday starts, for example **08:00**, and clear any other selected hours, including the default **09:00**. Keep **Minute** at **:00**. Select **Save automation**. The card shows the **Daily** trigger, and **Automation details** shows the **Schedule** and the **Next run** time.

pages.title: Why schedule?
pages.caption: A manual automation answers "What’s the status right now?" A scheduled automation answers "What changed since yesterday?" without requiring you to remember to ask. The app also supports **Hourly**, **Weekly**, and **CRON** schedules. CRON gives you the most control: the app validates the expression and shows a human-readable preview before you save.

pages.title: Event triggers
pages.caption: Schedules run on the clock. Event triggers run in response to something happening in the repository: **Issue**, **Automation failed**, **Automation completed**, **Code scanning alert**, **Dependabot alert**, **Discussion comment**, **Discussion opened**, **Discussion updated**, **Pull request**, **Secret scanning alert**, **Sub issue added**, and **Workflow**. The menu is longer than its window, so scroll it to see every choice.

pages.title: Keeping event triggers safe
pages.caption: Event-triggered automations react to external input. Start read-only. Limit repository scope to one repository. Filter by label or search query. Avoid write tools until the summary is reliable: a broad trigger paired with write tools increases prompt-injection risk. Review run history regularly.

pages.title: Cloud automations
pages.caption: Every automation you’ve created so far is local: it runs from your machine while the app is open. A cloud automation runs on GitHub-hosted infrastructure, so it can fire even when your laptop is closed. It needs Copilot cloud agent enabled, a private or internal repository, and billing: each run uses GitHub Actions minutes and AI credits. A fork of this public course repository is public, so read this section without creating a cloud automation.

pages.title: The Tools list
pages.caption: When you enable **Run in the cloud**, a **Tools** dropdown appears. Each selected tool grants the cloud agent a specific capability. Select only the tools the task requires: use **Search tools…**, or write your instructions first and select **Suggest tools**, then review the list. Below it, **Type** is **Personal** by default, or **Shared**. Personal does not make the resulting sessions private: keep secrets out of the prompt for both types.

pages.title: What Tidewheel’s keepers know
pages.caption: Every automation needs a trigger, prompt, tool set, and review path. Manual automations are the safest first step: test the prompt before adding a schedule. Scheduled automations answer "what changed since yesterday?" without requiring you to remember to ask. Apply least privilege: give an automation only the tools it needs, so untrusted issue or PR text is less able to steer the agent.

pages.title: Your turn: one manual automation
pages.caption: Create one manual automation for your own workflow. Name it clearly. Use a manual trigger. Write a prompt with one bounded task. Keep it read-only: in the prompt, tell it not to edit files, post comments, or change GitHub items. Run it once. Inspect the run history and revise the prompt. You succeed when you can explain why the automation is safe to run again.

pages.title: Course complete
pages.caption: You’ve gone from setup and orientation through sessions, worktrees, and context; the development-and-GitHub workflow loop; skills and custom agents; MCP servers and plugins; canvases; and automations. One habit stayed constant: keeping a human in control of quality and delivery. Human judgment stays in the loop at every major control point: before implementation starts, before a pull request is opened, and before any merge automation is enabled.

pages.title: A local automation does not run?
pages.caption: A local run happens only when your computer is awake and the GitHub Copilot app is running. Also confirm that the project is still connected and that the local tools and credentials that the prompt needs still work.

pages.title: The review readiness report is empty?
pages.caption: Confirm that the setup script finished and that your fork has open pull requests. Then check your repository permissions and any filters in the prompt.

pages.title: Cloud automations are unavailable?
pages.caption: Cloud automations are not available in public repositories, and a fork of this course is public. In a private or internal repository, check the organization policy, repository settings, billing, and the tools that you selected.

pages.title: A scheduled run is noisy?
pages.caption: Narrow the prompt, run the schedule less often, or add a label or branch filter to reduce the output.

pages.title: The automation made surprising suggestions?
pages.caption: Make the prompt more specific, and list what the automation must not do. For a cloud automation, also clear the tools that the task does not need.

glossary.definition: A saved agent task in the GitHub Copilot app that you run on demand or later on a schedule. It has a trigger, a prompt, tools, and a review path.
A manual automation runs only when you start it. It is the safest first step, because you can test the prompt before giving it a schedule or trigger.
Hostile text, for example in an issue title or body, that tries to steer the agent. A read-only automation with only the tools it needs reduces the risk.
An automation that runs on GitHub-hosted infrastructure, so it can fire even when your laptop is closed. It is not available in public repositories.
